= Bearers of the ''de Glasgu'' Name and the Emergence of the Glasgow Surname, c.1175–1506 =

<span id='summary'></span>
== Research summary ==

This page is a documentary register of medieval people recorded as '''de Glasgu''', '''de Glascu''', '''de Glasgw''', '''de Glasgeu''', '''de Glascou''', '''Glasgw''', “of Glasgow” and closely related forms. It separates direct personal locatives or bynames from descriptions of office, institution or venue, and it keeps disputed readings and proposed identity merges outside the core count.

{| class="wikitable"
|+ '''Current research position'''
! Question
! Finding
|-
| Earliest secure direct bearer
| [[#roger|Roger de Glasgu]], c.1175–1199
|-
| Direct working identities before 1300
| '''12''' — see the [[#register_pre1300|pre-1300 register]]
|-
| Personal byname or surname-function before 1400
| '''Demonstrated''' — strongest in [[#hugh|Hugh de Glasgw]], [[#william_corbridge|William de Glascou]] and [[#master_john|Master John de Glasgow]]
|-
| Repeated use by the same person
| '''Demonstrated'''
|-
| Family-identifying use
| '''Demonstrated''' — [[#alexander_son_robert|Alexander son of Robert de Glascu]] and [[#john_father_malcolm|Malcolm son of John de Glasgu]]
|-
| Hereditary transmission
| '''Not demonstrated'''
|-
| One pedigree joining the medieval bearers
| '''Not demonstrated'''
|-
| Provisional additional bearer
| [[#david_provisional|'''David de Glasgu''']] — probable thirteenth-century Lennox witness; not counted because the original act or printed page has not been recovered
|-
| End date
| 1506, because [[#john_alias_smith|John de Glasgow alias Smith]] is material to the transition from locative naming to later surname practice
|}

'''Bottom line.''' Glasgow was functioning before 1400 as a stable identifying second name for particular people. The evidence proves individual and family-identifying use; it does not yet prove that the name passed from one independently documented bearer to another as an inherited surname.

<span id='method'></span>
== Evidence framework, terminology and counting rules ==

Medieval second names should not automatically be treated as modern hereditary surnames. Twelfth- and thirteenth-century bynames could change between contexts or generations, and hereditary treatment requires positive evidence rather than retrospective capitalisation.<ref name="NamingMethodPoMS">Matthew Hammond, “Treatment of occupational by-names and surnames” (2013), People of Medieval Scotland editorial guidance, noting that most twelfth- and thirteenth-century occupational second names were technically bynames liable to change between generations and that hereditary treatment requires evidence; [https://poms-os.kdl.kcl.ac.uk/information/editorial-information/treatment-of-occupational-by-names-and-surnames-2013/ PoMS].</ref><ref name="HammondScot2012">Matthew Hammond, “The use of the name ‘Scot’ in the central middle ages, part two: ‘Scot’ as a Surname, north of the Firth of Forth”, Journal of Scottish Name Studies, vol. 6 (2012), pp. 11–50; [https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/92326/ University of Glasgow repository].</ref>

{| class="wikitable"
|+ '''Four evidential levels'''
! Level
! Test
! Status in this register
|-
| 1
| '''Direct personal locative or byname.''' The record attaches Glasgow to the person’s name rather than merely to an office, institution, residence or venue.
| '''Proved'''
|-
| 2
| '''Repeated use by the same person.''' The identification recurs across years, offices or documentary settings.
| '''Proved'''
|-
| 3
| '''Family-identifying use.''' A Glasgow-designated father is used to identify a son or another relative.
| '''Proved'''
|-
| 4
| '''Demonstrated hereditary transmission.''' Two independently documented relatives are each shown using Glasgow as their own name.
| '''Not proved'''
|}

The register follows these rules:

* a person is counted only when the syntax directly attaches the Glasgow form to that person;
* a son is not counted as a Glasgow bearer when the locative grammatically belongs only to his father;
* two texts preserving one accounting event count as one event, although both textual witnesses may affect confidence in a reading;
* identical forename and locative are not enough to merge records without a repeated office, associate, property, patron, relationship or other identifying bridge;
* assigned dates, retrospective notices, later cartulary copies and derivative modern transcriptions are labelled as such;
* '''secure''' means the reading and personal construction are clear; '''high confidence''' means a minor textual or identity issue remains; '''probable''' means the identification is persuasive but not proved; '''possible''' means chronologically or socially compatible only; and '''rejected''' means the proposed occurrence does not contain the claimed personal name.

The term '''surname-function''' is used only for a stable identifying second name. It does not imply inheritance. The safer default for isolated early examples is '''personal locative''' or '''byname'''.

<span id='provisional_bearers'></span>
== Provisional and unverified bearers ==

This section preserves promising leads that are not counted in the chronological register because the underlying act, manuscript or checkable printed page has not yet been recovered.

<span id='david_provisional'></span>
=== David de Glasgu ===

The exact form '''David de Glasgu''' is repeatedly reported for a witness to a charter or grant associated with Lennox or Levenax and apparently derived from the documentary tradition represented by the ''Cartularium Comitatus de Levenax''. The combination of the exact personal locative, a witness role and a specific regional charter tradition makes David a '''probable additional pre-1450 bearer'''.

The evidential limit is important. No charter number, manuscript reference or checkable printed page has yet been recovered, and the online notices may all derive from one secondary surname notice rather than independent sightings. David is therefore '''provisional and excluded from the core count'''. His period can presently be described only as probably thirteenth century.

No record located in the present search calls David the son, brother, heir or kinsman of another ''de Glasgu'' bearer. He should not be attached to Roger, Malcolm, William, John, Adam or anyone else in the register.

The same search found no source-specific personal-surname evidence strong enough to add Agnes, Bartholomew, Henry, Herbert, Maurice, Nicholas, Patrick, Peter, Simon, Stephen or Thomas. Hits describing a cleric or other person as ''Glasguensis'', or as belonging to the city or diocese of Glasgow, are institutional or geographical descriptions rather than the surname '''de Glasgu'''.

<span id='profiles'></span>
== Bearer profiles and core source findings ==

Profiles are grouped chronologically. Use the [[#people_index|people index]] or [[#register|register]] to jump directly to a bearer.

<span id='profiles_1175_1249'></span>
=== c.1175–1249: Glasgow, Dublin and the early Robert problem ===

<span id='roger'></span>
==== Roger de Glasgu, c.1175–1199 ====

A charter assigned to Bishop Jocelin’s episcopate records Brother Raan Corbeht, master of the Templars in Scotland, confirming to William Gley of Glasgow a toft in the burgh and fishing rights in the Clyde. The witness list includes ''Rogero de Glasgu''.<ref name="RogerREG">Cosmo Innes, ed., ''Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis'', vol. I (Edinburgh, 1843), no. 41, pp. 37–38; vol. II, index under “Glasgu, Rogerus de”; [https://archive.org/details/registrumepiscv175glasuoft Internet Archive].</ref>

The same list separately names ''fratre Rogero Elemosynar'', Brother Roger the almoner. Roger de Glasgu was therefore another man. He is not styled brother and is given no office.

John, clerk of the bishop of Glasgow, also witnesses the act. People of Medieval Scotland identifies that clerk as John of Huntingdon, later an Official of Glasgow, and records Roger separately.<ref name="RogerPoMS">People of Medieval Scotland, Knights Templar of Balantrodoch, person no. 4968, transaction concerning William Gley’s Glasgow toft and Clyde fishery; Roger of Glasgow is linked separately as person no. 8789; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/4968/ PoMS].</ref> Co-witnessing places Roger within a Glasgow-centred institutional network; it does not establish kinship or household membership.

A later Glasgow act of 1201×1202 names an otherwise unqualified Roger among the cathedral vicars, again in the company of John of Huntingdon.<ref name="RogerVicar">Cosmo Innes, ed., ''Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis'', vol. I (Edinburgh, 1843), no. 95, p. 83; vol. II, index under “Rogerus, vicarius”; [https://archive.org/details/registrumepiscv175glasuoft Internet Archive].</ref> The repeated associate makes identity possible, but the later witness has no locative or other identifier. The secure record remains the c.1175–1199 charter; the vicar is a possible later occurrence only.

<span id='dublin_cluster'></span>
==== The Dublin guild cluster ====

The complete ''Dublin Guild Merchant Roll'' contains four Glasgow-associated entries:

{| class="wikitable"
! Entry
! Date and roll position
! What the record shows
! Evidential limit
|-
| <span id='richard_dublin'></span>'''Richard de Glasgu'''
| probably late twelfth century; membrane 2d/B
| Guild merchant admission; paid 8 shillings
| Relationship to the adjacent Robert is not stated
|-
| <span id='robert_dublin'></span>'''Robert de Glasgu'''
| probably late twelfth century; membrane 2d/B
| Guild merchant admission immediately after Richard; paid 8 shillings
| He may be Alexander’s father, but the roll does not identify him as such
|-
| <span id='gilbert_dublin'></span>'''Gilbert or Gilibertus de Glascu'''
| before 1222/23; membrane 11d/B
| Guild merchant admission; paid 8 shillings
| No relationship to Richard or Robert is stated
|-
| <span id='alexander_son_robert'></span>'''Alexander, son of Robert de Glascu'''
| 1238/39; membrane 27/B
| Explicit father-son formula
| The Latin attaches ''de Glascu'' to Robert, not necessarily to Alexander
|}

Patricia Becker’s improved place-name index confirms all four and assigns them to Glasgow, Lanarkshire, Scotland.<ref name="BeckerIndex">Patricia Becker, “An Analysis of the Dublin Guild Merchant Roll c.1190–1265” (M.Phil. thesis, Trinity College Dublin, 1996), appendix and improved place-name index; [https://www.tara.tcd.ie/items/7e36bba9-c81a-4964-8eba-58e1c682a323 Trinity College Dublin repository] and [https://www.tara.tcd.ie/bitstreams/005632d1-a582-4fb1-9278-99a49552ea92/download appendix PDF].</ref> The complete roll’s place index likewise identifies ''Glascu'' and ''Glasgu'' with Glasgow and lists Gloucester under separate forms.<ref name="DublinPlaces">Philomena Connolly and Geoffrey Martin, eds., ''The Dublin Guild Merchant Roll, c.1190–1265'' (Dublin: Dublin Corporation, 1992), index of places, identifying ''Glascu'' and ''Glasgu'' with Glasgow, Scotland and listing Gloucester separately; [https://www.johngrenham.com/dcla/dmgr/places.php Dublin City Library and Archive digital transcript].</ref> No fifth Glasgow entry has been identified in the complete indexed roll.

Richard and Robert occur consecutively and each paid eight shillings. Gilbert paid the same sum. Alexander appears in the dated admissions for 1238/39.<ref name="DublinGuild">Philomena Connolly and Geoffrey Martin, eds., ''The Dublin Guild Merchant Roll, c.1190–1265'' (Dublin: Dublin Corporation, 1992), membrane 2d/B; Dublin City Library and Archive, transcript by Philomena Connolly; [https://www.johngrenham.com/dcla/dmgr/browse.php?image_order=8 online transcript].</ref><ref name="DublinGilbert">Connolly and Martin, ''Dublin Guild Merchant Roll'', membrane 11d/B; [https://www.johngrenham.com/dcla/dmgr/browse.php?image_order=22 online transcript].</ref><ref name="DublinAlexander">Connolly and Martin, ''Dublin Guild Merchant Roll'', membrane 27/B, admissions for 1238/39; [https://www.johngrenham.com/dcla/dmgr/browse.php?image_order=41 online transcript].</ref> The evidence establishes repeated Glasgow-associated participation in the guild. It does not define kinship among Richard, Robert and Gilbert.

The early membranes were copied from an earlier source, so adjacency cannot prove simultaneous admission, joint travel, partnership or household membership.<ref name="DublinGuildEditorial">Connolly and Martin, ''Dublin Guild Merchant Roll'', editorial note; [https://www.johngrenham.com/dcla/dmgr/about.php Dublin City Library and Archive digital edition].</ref> Robert of Renfrew immediately follows Richard and Robert, and Philip of Irvine occurs nearby. That pattern is compatible with a west-Scottish trading association, but it remains contextual evidence rather than a pedigree.

Alexander de Grenoc should not be treated as Alexander of Greenock. Becker’s revised index assigns him and the relevant cluster of ''Grenoc/Grenok'' forms to Greenogue, County Meath. The index separately recognises Greenock, Scotland under other entries, showing that the distinction was deliberate.<ref name="BeckerIndex" />

The father named in 1238/39 may be the earlier Dublin guild Robert. The chronology permits that identification, but the record does not say “the aforesaid Robert”, repeat an occupation or property, or supply another identifying bridge. The father could also be [[#robert_1200|the Robert in the 1200 plea roll]], [[#robert_dunkeld|the Dunkeld clerk]], [[#robert_durham|the Durham witness]] or a fifth, otherwise unrecorded Robert.

<span id='robert_1200'></span>
==== Robert de Glascu in the Curia Regis roll, 1200 ====

The printed Curia Regis roll for Michaelmas term, 2 John, names '''Robert de Glascu''' among men said to have been present at a robbery at ''Dadinton''. It notes that he had poor eyesight and could not open his eyes well. The concluding wording appears to say collectively that the men were well dressed and had wives.<ref name="RobertCuria1200">C. T. Flower, ed., ''Curia Regis Rolls of the Reigns of Richard I and John'', vol. I, Richard I–2 John (London: HMSO, 1922), p. 354, TNA KB 26/22, m. 1, Michaelmas term, 2 John (1200), naming ''Rob<sup>us</sup> de Glascu''; [https://books.google.com/books?id=SWRnAAAAMAAJ Google Books]. See also Paul Hyams, “Orality and Literacy in the Age of the Angevin Law Reforms,” in Richard W. Kaeuper, Paul Dingman and Peter Sposato, eds., ''Law, Governance, and Justice: New Views on Medieval Constitutionalism'' (Leiden: Brill, 2013), pp. 27–71, at p. 43 n. 48, doi:10.1163/9789004236424_004; [https://brill.com/display/book/edcoll/9789004236424/B9789004236424_004.xml Brill].</ref>

The notice does not establish Robert’s occupation, residence or precise procedural status. He should not be called a convicted robber, formal witness or merchant unless the original roll or fuller process supplies that information. “Named among men said to have been present at a robbery” is the defensible description.

The form ''Glascu'' is independently identified with Glasgow in the Dublin place index, which distinguishes Gloucester. That makes Glasgow the high-confidence reading here, although the English plea roll itself does not gloss the place-name.

The printed edition and a modern legal-historical discussion both support the occurrence, but TNA KB 26/22, membrane 1, has not been re-examined for this revision. The manuscript remains a priority for checking abbreviation, marginalia and any wording omitted by the edition.

The Dunkeld charter names ''Roberto de Glasgu'' among Bishop Gilbert’s clerks.<ref name="RobertDunkeld">D. E. Easson and Angus Macdonald, eds., ''Charters of the Abbey of Inchcolm'' (Edinburgh: Scottish History Society, 1938), no. XIV, pp. 12–13 and notes pp. 119–21. The expanded witness list containing ''Roberto de Glasgu'' survives in the 1423 transumpt; the editors note “Not identified”; [https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1283/0085/128300859.23.pdf National Library of Scotland].</ref> Its expanded witness list survives in a 1423 transumpt, so the reading is usable but not contemporary autograph evidence. The wider witness group shows genuine connections between the churches of Glasgow and Dunkeld.<ref name="GlasgowDunkeldNetwork">Easson and Macdonald, ''Charters of the Abbey of Inchcolm'', notes to no. XIV, pp. 120–21.</ref>

The Durham ordinance directly names ''dominis Roberto de Glascu'' in a witness list and is internally dated at Kippax on 30 January 1248, conventionally 1248/49.<ref name="RobertDurham1249">DEEDS, charter 03320015, ''Durham 1241–1283'', vol. 29, transcribing Durham Cathedral Archive, Register II, fol. 321v.; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/03320015 DEEDS 03320015].</ref> Robert is styled ''dominus'', but the act does not state his office. The ecclesiastical context makes clerical status plausible; it does not justify calling him a priest, canon or episcopal clerk without another source.

The date and episcopal setting allow [[#robert_dunkeld|the Dunkeld]] and [[#robert_durham|the Durham]] records to concern one man. They do not prove it. No shared benefice, patron, repeated associate or office currently joins them.

<small>[[#people_index|↑ People index]] · [[#register_pre1300|Pre-1300 register]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='profiles_1259_1299'></span>
=== 1259–1299: clerical, civic and royal bearers ===

<span id='john_gamelin'></span>
==== John de Glasgu, Bishop Gamelin’s chaplain, and the Dunipace problem ====

A St Andrews act dated 2 February 1259 names ''domino Johanne de Glasgu, capellano domini episcopi'' — John de Glasgu, chaplain of Bishop Gamelin.<ref name="JohnGamelin">''Registrum Prioratus Sancti Andree'' (Bannatyne Club, Edinburgh, 1841), p. 173; [https://archive.org/details/libercartarump6900edinuoft Internet Archive]. See also People of Medieval Scotland, person no. 3404 and transaction factoid no. 15755, dating the renewal of Lathrisk and Kettle to 2 February 1259; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/3404/ PoMS].</ref> The source does not identify his parents or call him Gamelin’s brother.

A broad-dated Cambuskenneth charter concerning Dunipace also includes ''Johanne de Glasgu''. Its witness list contains Richard de Stickley, who appears with John in the 1259 act as the bishop’s steward.<ref name="CambusJohn">''Registrum Monasterii S. Marie de Cambuskenneth'', no. 81; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/07280081 DEEDS 07280081]. See also People of Medieval Scotland, source no. 5639, suggesting a probable date in the 1250s or 1260s; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/source/5639/ PoMS].</ref> The repeated, relatively distinctive associate and the likely 1250s–1260s dating make it probable that the Dunipace witness was Gamelin’s chaplain.

The Dunipace act does not repeat John’s office, so the identification is not certain. Database allocations should not be treated as proof where the underlying records remain ambiguous. This John therefore remains separate from [[#john_holyrood|the Holyrood John of 1299]].

<span id='hugh'></span>
==== Hugh de Glasgw in Glasgow, c.1283 ====

A lay quitclaim concerning three perticates of land in Glasgow’s Rottenrow names the serving bailies and then ''Hugone de Glasgw'' among the witnesses.<ref name="Hugh1283">''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'', no. 341, lay quitclaim assigned to 1283; [https://deeds.utsc.utoronto.ca/charters/06190339 DEEDS 06190339].</ref> The act is assigned to 1283 rather than internally dated. Its position within a connected group of Rottenrow deeds makes c.1283 a reasonable working date.<ref name="HughDossier">''Syllabus of Scottish Cartularies: Paisley'', discussion of ''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'', nos. 339–343; [https://scottishmedievalcharters.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/paisley.pdf PDF].</ref>

This is one of the strongest pre-1300 examples of personal byname function. The instrument already states that the land lay within the burgh of Glasgow, refers to Glasgow’s bailies, and uses the town seal. The scribe nevertheless distinguishes Hugh personally as ''de Glasgw''. The phrase is therefore doing more than stating the venue.

Hugh has no stated occupation, office, parentage or property interest. He appears in a lay urban transaction, but the source does not expressly call him a burgess, landholder, neighbour or resident. Those descriptions should not be supplied as facts.

The text survives through the Paisley cartulary, probably compiled in the sixteenth century from earlier instruments.<ref name="HughMS">National Library of Scotland, Adv.MS.34.4.14, Paisley Abbey cartulary; [https://digital.nls.uk/early-manuscripts/browse/archive/229918103 manuscript description].</ref> The reading is clear in the printed and digital transcription, but the exact thirteenth-century spelling is not autograph.

<span id='alexander_escheator'></span>
==== Alexander de Glasgu or de Glasgow, royal escheator, 1289/90 ====

A Scottish Exchequer account records money received ''per manum Alexandri de Glasgow, escaetoris'' — through the hand of Alexander de Glasgow, escheator.<ref name="AlexanderER">John Stuart and George Burnett, eds., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. I, A.D. 1264–1359 (Edinburgh, 1878), p. 47 and index; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir01scot Internet Archive]. See also [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/18712/ PoMS].</ref> This directly corrects the often-repeated secondary form “Andrew de Glasgow”.<ref name="AlexanderNameCorrection">John Stuart and George Burnett, eds., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. I, A.D. 1264–1359 (Edinburgh, 1878), p. 47 and index; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir01scot Internet Archive].</ref>

Joseph Stevenson transcribed a damaged receipt dated 7 March 1289/90 as ''Alexandri de Glasgu''.<ref name="AlexanderStevenson">Joseph Stevenson, ed., ''Documents Illustrative of the History of Scotland'', vol. I (Edinburgh, 1870), transcription of the damaged original receipt dated 7 March 1289/90, reading ''Alexandri de Glasgu''.</ref> Joseph Bain later calendared the damaged instrument as ''Alexander de Glasfrith (?)'', with an explicit question mark.<ref name="AlexanderGlasfrith">Joseph Bain, ed., ''Calendar of Documents Relating to Scotland'', vol. II (Edinburgh, 1884), no. 409, p. 100, uncertain reading ''Alexander de Glasfrith (?)''; index under “Glasford”; [https://archive.org/details/calendarofdocume02edin Internet Archive].</ref> The separate Exchequer text is not dependent on Bain’s reading and clearly gives ''de Glasgow''.

The best current treatment is therefore '''Alexander de Glasgu or de Glasgow, high confidence''', with ''Glasfrith/Glassford'' retained as a disputed reading of the damaged receipt. A modern image of the original is still needed before the palaeographical issue can be closed.

The office places Alexander in royal administration south of the Forth. No source identifies his family, residence or relationship to [[#alexander_son_robert|Alexander son of Robert de Glascu in Dublin]].

<span id='walter'></span>
==== Master Walter de Glasgu, c.1291 ====

Melrose charter material names '''Master Walter de Glasgu''' as a witness around 1291.<ref name="Walter1291">''Liber Sancte Marie de Melros'', charter no. 353 and associated digital data; [https://archive.researchdata.leeds.ac.uk/574/ University of Leeds]. See also [https://www.poms.ac.uk/record/person/16434/ PoMS].</ref> “Master” indicates recognised advanced education or academic standing. No alternative byname or further secure occurrence has been located.

<span id='john_holyrood'></span>
==== John of Glasgow, Holyrood religious, 1299 ====

A John of Glasgow appears among the Holyrood community which swore fealty to Edward I on 7 January 1299.<ref name="HolyroodJohn">Joseph Bain, ed., ''Calendar of Documents Relating to Scotland'', vol. II (Edinburgh, 1884), no. 1052; [https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/14528/ PoMS].</ref> Forty years separate this record from Gamelin’s chaplaincy. An elderly former chaplain later entering an Augustinian community is possible, but no office, patron, associate, property or explicit alias joins the records. The Holyrood John remains separate.

<small>[[#people_index|↑ People index]] · [[#register_pre1300|Pre-1300 register]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='profiles_1312_1419'></span>
=== 1312–1419: monastic, royal, medical and episcopal records ===

<span id='richard_arbroath'></span>
==== Richard of Glasgow, monk of Arbroath, 1312 ====

A record dated 3 July 1312 names '''Richard of Glasgow''' among the Arbroath community.<ref name="Richard1312">[https://poms.ac.uk/record/person/16356/ PoMS, Richard of Glasgow, monk], citing the Arbroath register.</ref> It is a direct personal locative and confirms continuity of the form after 1300. No relationship to the earlier Dublin Richard is implied by the shared forename.

<span id='william_corbridge'></span>
==== William de Glascou, vicar of Corbridge, 1315–1322 ====

On 20 November 1315 Bishop Richard de Kellawe instituted ''Willelmo de Glasgow, capellano'' as perpetual vicar of Corbridge after an inquiry into the vacancy and the presentee’s suitability.<ref name="WilliamCorbridge1315Full">''Registrum Palatinum Dunelmense'', vol. II, pp. 759–60; [https://archive.org/details/registrumpalati00kellgoog Internet Archive].</ref> William later witnessed a deed dated 19 November 1322 as ''domino Willelmo de Glascou vicario de Corbrygge''.<ref name="WilliamCorbridge1322">''A History of Northumberland'', vol. X, deed dated 19 November 1322; [https://archive.org/details/historyofnorthum10nort Internet Archive].</ref>

The syntax is important. ''de Glasgow/de Glascou'' is William’s personal designation; ''capellano'' and ''vicario de Corbrygge'' separately state his clerical status and office. The name recurs seven years apart while the benefice is independently specified. This proves repeated personal byname or surname-function. It does not prove that William inherited or transmitted the name.

<span id='adam_berwick'></span>
==== Adam de Glasgeu, burgess of Berwick, probably fourteenth century ====

An undated Melrose charter begins ''ego Adam de Glasgeu, burgensis burgi Berwici super Twedam''. Adam granted Melrose Abbey ten acres called Hiddeslaw in the tenement of Bondington beside Berwick-upon-Tweed.<ref name="AdamGlasgeu">Cosmo Innes, ed., ''Liber Sancte Marie de Melros: Munimenta Vetustiora Monasterii Cisterciensis de Melros'', vol. 2 (Edinburgh, 1837), Appendix no. 25, p. 688; [https://saints.hca.ed.ac.uk/entry/EN/JD/3830 Adam de Glasgeu] and [https://saints.hca.ed.ac.uk/document/DO/JD/2961 document record].</ref>

The specialist database classifies the deed as possibly fourteenth century, but no narrower date is established. Adam should not be counted among the pre-1300 bearers without new palaeographical or archival evidence.

The warranty clause binds Adam and his heirs, as medieval conveyancing commonly did. It shows an alienable interest in the land; it does not identify an heir, prove that Adam had children or show an heir using the Glasgow name.

<span id='john_1343'></span>
==== John de Glasgu, royal-account payee, 1343 ====

An Exchequer account records 7s. 6d. paid to ''Johanni de Glasgu, pro mensa quorundam serviencium regis''.<ref name="John1343">''Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. I, p. 531; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir01scot Internet Archive].</ref> The entry concerns the board or table of royal servants but does not name John’s office. “Caterer”, “steward” or another precise occupation would be conjectural.

Thirty-four years separate this payment from the first secure record of [[#master_john|Master John, chancellor of Dunkeld]]. No repeated office, associate, benefice or patron links them. The 1343 payee remains separate.

<span id='master_john'></span>
==== Master John de Glasgow, 1377–1419 ====

Master John is the strongest extended example of pre-1400 surname-function. The secure core begins with two records naming the same man and office:

* 24 January 1377: ''Johanne de Glasgu cancellario ecclesie Dunkeldensis'' in a Glasgow episcopal charter;<ref name="John1377">''Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis'', vol. I, p. 292; [https://archive.org/details/registrumepiscv175glasuoft Internet Archive].</ref>
* 2 June 1384: the same personal name and chancellorship in a Paisley instrument made at Dumbarton.<ref name="JohnDumbarton1384">''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'' (Edinburgh, 1832), p. 331, instrument dated 2 June 1384; [https://archive.org/details/registrummonaste00mait Internet Archive].</ref>

The identical office makes this a high-confidence seven-year identity. In both records, ''de Glasgu'' is grammatically separate from ''chancellor of the church of Dunkeld''.

Two safe-conduct entries dated 18 February 1379/80 and 7 December 1380 include John de Glasgow and Master John de Glasgow. They fit the chancellor’s chronology and academic standing.<ref name="JohnSafeConducts1380">Robert Nicholson, A Reconsideration of the influence of John Wycliffe, Wycliffism, Lollardy and Hussitism, upon 15th Century Scotland (M.Res. thesis, University of the Highlands and Islands, 2024), appendix of safe-conduct names, entries for 18 February 1379/80 and 7 December 1380. The appendix states that it transcribes T. M. A. MacNab’s 1933 thesis and cross-references D. E. R. Watt; it is used here as a secondary locator pending verification in Rotuli Scotiae or the underlying enrolments; [https://pureadmin.uhi.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/54736571/Robert_Nicholson_thesis.pdf UHI Research Database].</ref> The current citation, however, is a modern thesis appendix derived from an earlier unpublished thesis and cross-referenced to Watt. It is a useful locator, not an adequate final substitute for checking ''Rotuli Scotiae'' or the underlying enrolment. The entries should therefore remain in the working reconstruction but be flagged for primary verification.

A Glasgow cathedral instrument dated 19 October 1388 names ''Johanne de Glasgw canonico Aberdonensi''.<ref name="JohnAberdeen1388">''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'' (Edinburgh, 1832), p. 340, instrument dated 19 October 1388; [https://archive.org/details/registrummonaste00mait Internet Archive].</ref> Name, date, senior clerical status and Glasgow setting make identity with the former Dunkeld chancellor probable. The record does not repeat the chancellorship or provide an explicit alias, so this component should not be described as certain.

Later papal evidence says that John exchanged the Dunkeld canonry, prebend and chancellorship with John Lang for the vicarage of Obney or Auchtergaven around 1387 and that John belonged to Cardinal Walter Wardlaw’s household.<ref name="JohnLang1413">''Petitions to the Pope, 1342–1419'', petition of John Lang, granted 19 August 1413; [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/pp594-612 British History Online].</ref><ref name="JohnRetro1405">''Petitions to the Pope, 1342–1419'', Petitions, vol. XCVIII, petition of John de Retro, granted at Genoa, 24 May 1405.</ref> These notices are later and retrospective but materially strengthen the career reconstruction.

John was styled canon of Moray in 1404, included in a safe-conduct in 1406 and named as a priest acting in a legal or proctorial case in 1412.<ref name="JohnMoray">''Charters of the Abbey of Coupar Angus'', vol. II, instrument of 14 November 1404, naming ''Johanne de Glasgw canonico Morauiensi''; [https://digital.nls.uk/scottish-history-society-publications/browse/archive/126771087?mode=transcription National Library of Scotland].</ref><ref name="JohnSafeConduct1406">Sir Thomas Duffus Hardy, ed., ''Syllabus (in English) of the Documents Relating to England and Other Kingdoms Contained in the Collection Known as “Rymer’s Foedera”'', vol. II, 1377–1654 (London, 1873), p. 556, entry dated 5 July 1406; [https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_835JAAAAYAAJ Internet Archive].</ref><ref name="John1412">Papal record concerning Thomas Traill, 17 August 1412; [https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1266/1368/126613685.23.pdf National Library of Scotland].</ref> Obney was described as vacant by his death outside the Roman Curia on 2 May 1419; a 1425 petition again referred to his death.<ref name="JohnDeath1419">E. R. Lindsay and A. I. Cameron, eds., ''Calendar of Scottish Supplications to Rome, 1418–1422'' (Edinburgh, 1934), p. 39.</ref><ref name="John1425">''Calendar of Scottish Supplications to Rome'', petition of John Malcolmi, Rome, 8 Id. September, year 8, register 190, fol. 46.</ref>

The career should be counted by evidential group rather than compressed into “twelve pre-1400 records”:

{| class="wikitable"
! Group
! Occurrences
! Dates
|-
| Explicit contemporary occurrences before 1400
| 5 working occurrences
| 1377; 1379/80; 1380; 1384; probable 1388
|-
| Later retrospective evidence about the pre-1400 exchange
| 2
| 1405; 1413
|-
| Contemporary occurrences after 1400
| 3
| 1404; 1406; 1412
|-
| Death and posthumous notices
| 2
| 1419; 1425
|}

The total working reconstruction contains twelve documentary occurrences. That count depends on retaining the probable 1388 identification and the two safe-conducts pending primary verification. The secure core remains strong even if one of those components is later split.

<span id='matthew'></span>
==== Matthew de Glasgu, 1384 ====

A papal petition granted at Avignon on 20 December 1384 records '''Matthew de Glasgu''' seeking a benefice in the gift of the abbot and convent of Kelso.<ref name="Matthew1384">William Henry Bliss, ed., ''Calendar of Entries in the Papal Registers Relating to Great Britain and Ireland: Petitions to the Pope'', vol. I, A.D. 1342–1419 (London, 1896), p. 566, Petitions, vol. LXIII, fol. 85; [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/p566a British History Online].</ref> The calendar gives no diocese, degree, office, patronymic, existing benefice or parish sought.

Matthew de Glendonwyn belongs to a compatible generation and ecclesiastical environment, but no record yet uses both names or supplies an identifying bridge. Matthew de Glasgu is a genuine bearer; the Glendonwyn comparison is a possible identity hypothesis only.

<span id='william_priest'></span>
==== William de Glasgu, priest, 1394 ====

Two papal-calendar entries in 1394 name William de Glasgu seeking benefices in the gifts of Kelso and Kilwinning; one explicitly calls him a priest.<ref name="WilliamKelso1394">''Petitions to the Pope, 1342–1419'', roll of Matthew, bishop of Glasgow, entry for William de Glasgu, priest; [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/pp588-590 British History Online].</ref><ref name="WilliamKilwinning1394">''Petitions to the Pope, 1342–1419'', “Volume LXXXIX: 1 Benedict XIII”, coronation roll, entry for William de Glasgu; [https://www.british-history.ac.uk/no-series/petitions-to-pope/1342-1419/pp612-614 British History Online].</ref> The identical name and year make one man likely, but the calendars do not provide enough detail to make the merge absolute.

He is kept separate from [[#william_physician|the physician recorded in 1395 and 1397]]. A physician could also be a cleric, but no benefice, patron, office or transaction joins the records.

<span id='john_father_malcolm'></span>
==== John de Glasgu, father of Malcolm, 1394 ====

An Exchequer account rendered at Perth on 26 March 1394 records ''Malcolmo filio Johannis de Glasgu, pro debito regis''.<ref name="MalcolmSonJohn1394">George Burnett, ed., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. III, A.D. 1379–1406 (Edinburgh, 1880), p. 342; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir03grea Internet Archive].</ref> The grammar directly identifies John as ''de Glasgu'' and Malcolm as his son.

This is secure Scottish family-identifying use. It does not style Malcolm ''de Glasgu''. No office, property or associate connects the father with [[#john_1343|the 1343 payee]] or [[#master_john|Master John]], so he remains a separate working identity.

<span id='william_physician'></span>
==== William, physician de Glasgu, 1395–1397 ====

A Linlithgow customs account rendered on 30 March 1395 records a royal remission to ''Willelmo, medico de Glasgu'' on the custom of two sacks of wool.<ref name="WilliamPhysician1395">George Burnett, ed., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. III, p. 356, account rendered 30 March 1395; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir03grea Internet Archive].</ref> A chamberlain’s account rendered on 3 June 1397 records ''Willelmo, medico, de Glasgu, de dono regis'' and a royal gift of the same amount.<ref name="WilliamPhysician1397">George Burnett, ed., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. III, p. 427, chamberlain’s account rendered 3 June 1397; [https://archive.org/details/rotuliscaccariir03grea Internet Archive].</ref>

The repeated forename, occupation and locative within two years make one man highly probable. The punctuation and word order show that ''de Glasgu'' is a personal geographical identifier distinct from ''medicus''. The records do not show whether it was inherited, and they do not identify him with [[#william_priest|the priest petitioning in 1394]].

<small>[[#people_index|↑ People index]] · [[#register_1300_1419|Fourteenth-century register]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='profiles_1447_1506'></span>
=== 1447–1506: fixed forms and dual identification ===

<span id='john_glasgow_1447'></span>
==== John de Glasgu in Glasgow, 1447–1455 ====

John de Glasgu was a burgess of Glasgow by 21 June 1447, when he witnessed a Walkergate property transaction. He again witnessed a Glasgow property act on 10 April 1455.<ref name="John1447">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine: Munimenta Fratrum Predicatorum de Glasgu'' (Glasgow, 1846), act dated 21 June 1447; [https://archive.org/details/libercollegiino00annegoog Internet Archive].</ref><ref name="John1455">''Liber Collegii Nostre Domine'', act dated April 1455; [https://archive.org/details/libercollegiino00annegoog Internet Archive].</ref> Shared city, role and an eight-year interval make these very probably one man.

No document connects him with [[#john_stirling|the Stirling witness of the 1470s]]. The two clusters should not be merged merely because both men were called John Glasgow.

<span id='john_stirling'></span>
==== John Glasgw in Stirling, 1475–1479/80 ====

John Glasgw witnessed Stirling acts on 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80.<ref name="StirlingJohn">''Charters and Other Documents Relating to the Royal Burgh of Stirling, A.D. 1124–1705'' (Glasgow, 1884), acts dated 11 April 1475 and 2 March 1479/80; [https://archive.org/details/chartersotherdoc00stir Internet Archive].</ref> The shared town, name and short interval support one working identity. The unprefixed form is consistent with a more stabilised surname, but it does not itself establish descent from [[#john_glasgow_1447|the Glasgow burgess]] or any earlier bearer.

<span id='alan'></span>
==== Alan Glasgw, killed before 26 February 1495 ====

At the Jedburgh justice ayre on 26 February 1495, James Pilmure, described as ''in Ednem'', produced a remission which included “the Slaughter of Alan Glasgw”. Ralph Ker became surety that Pilmure would satisfy the injured parties.<ref name="Alan1495">Robert Pitcairn, ed., ''Criminal Trials in Scotland, from A.D. M.CCCC.LXXXVIII to A.D. M.DC.XXIV'', vol. I, part I (Edinburgh, 1833), p. 19. Pitcairn’s printed “1594–5” is a typographical error for 1494–5; the entry belongs to the second day of the Jedburgh ayre, 26 February 1495. Pitcairn describes Pilmure as ''in Ednem'', not “of Ednam”.</ref>

The entry names Alan only as the victim. It gives no residence, occupation, patronymic, widow, heir, motive, place or date of death. The offence appears as a separate item and should not be conflated with the preceding case involving George Smythe.

The underlying court book is NRS JC1/1.<ref name="JC11">National Records of Scotland, JC1/1, Court Books, old series, South Circuit and Edinburgh, 7 November 1493–13 August 1504.</ref> Published references place nearby Jedburgh business in folios 27v–28r, but Alan’s exact folio remains to be established.<ref name="Armstrong2013">Jackson W. Armstrong, “The Justice Ayre in the Border Sheriffdoms, 1493–1498”, ''Scottish Historical Review'', vol. 92, no. 1 (2013), pp. 1–37, including references to NRS JC1/1, fols. 27v–28r; doi:10.3366/shr.2013.0136.</ref> NLS Adv. MS. 6.1.4 is a c.1809 transcript of the contemporary court material, not a contemporary transcript.<ref name="NLSAdv614">National Library of Scotland, Adv. MS. 6.1.4, transcript, circa 1809, of Scottish justiciary court records covering November 1493–August 1504.</ref>

Pitcairn’s unprefixed ''Glasgw'' is good evidence of the printed form. The original Latin entry should still be checked before the absence of ''de'' is treated as conclusive manuscript evidence.

<span id='john_alias_smith'></span>
==== John de Glasgow alias Smith, 1506 ====

An instrument dated 28 April 1506 records Sir Allan Smith and '''John de Glasgow alias Smith''' as joint acquirers of a four-shilling annual rent from a tenement on Glasgow High Street.<ref name="JohnAliasSmith">Glasgow University Archives, Blackhouse Charters, GUA BL/204, formerly GUA 16403, instrument dated 28 April 1506.</ref>

The catalogue assigns the alias to John and states neither kinship with Allan nor occupation. ''Smith'' may have been inherited, occupational, maternal, household-based or otherwise established; the document does not decide which. The record should be indexed under both Glasgow and Smith.

The alias is evidence against a simple, unbroken single-name narrative. It does not support the unsupported “King’s armourer” theory without a royal-account, craft or occupational source.

<small>[[#people_index|↑ People index]] · [[#register_1447_1506|Late register]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='disputed_controls'></span>
== Disputed readings, rejected claims and controls ==

These cases are kept beside the register so that common transcription errors, false surname hits and institutional descriptions do not drift back into the bearer count.

<span id='disputed_readings'></span>
=== Disputed readings and transcription errors ===

<span id='alexander_disputed'></span>
==== Alexander: ''Glasgu/Glasgow'' versus ''Glasfrith (?)'' ====

The Exchequer account directly reads ''Alexandri de Glasgow''. Stevenson reported ''Alexandri de Glasgu'' from the damaged receipt; Bain later gave ''Alexander de Glasfrith (?)''. The Glasgow readings are therefore preferred, while the damaged original remains the final palaeographical test. ''Glasfrith/Glassford'' should not be presented as a separate bearer.

<span id='andrew_error'></span>
==== “Andrew de Glasgow”, 1289/90 ====

The Exchequer account names '''Alexander''', not Andrew. “Andrew de Glasgow” is a secondary error and not another person.<ref name="AlexanderNameCorrection" />

<span id='ragman_claim'></span>
==== Alleged Johan or John de Glasgu in the Ragman Roll, 1296 ====

The complete printed text and index do not contain the claimed Johan de Glasgu. They contain ''Johan del Glan'' and nearby Glasgow institutional entries, including Aleyn, vicar of Glasgow.<ref name="RagmanCorrection">Thomas Thomson, ed., ''Instrumenta Publica sive Processus super Fidelitatibus et Homagiis Scotorum Domino Regi Angliae Factis, A.D. MCCXCI–MCCXCVI'' (Bannatyne Club, Edinburgh, 1834), text and index under ''Glan'', ''Glafcu'' and ''Glafcuensis''; [https://archive.org/details/instrumentapublica00thomuoft Internet Archive].</ref> The modern claim is best treated as a conflation or misreading and rejected unless a manuscript witness is produced.

<span id='non_surname_controls'></span>
=== Non-surname controls ===

<span id='alan_vicar'></span>
==== Alan or Aleyn, vicar of Glasgow, 1296 ====

''Aleyn vicaire de Glafcu'' identifies Alan’s office as vicar of Glasgow. It does not call him Alan de Glasgow and is not surname evidence.

<span id='william_gley'></span>
==== William Gley of Glasgow, late twelfth century ====

The charter distinguishes ''Willelmus Gley de Glasg'' from the witness ''Rogero de Glasgu''. William’s identifying name is Gley; Glasgow describes him or the context. He should not be counted as a Glasgow bearer.<ref name="WilliamGley">Cosmo Innes, ed., ''Registrum Episcopatus Glasguensis'', vol. I (Edinburgh, 1843), no. 41, p. 37; [https://archive.org/details/registrumepiscv175glasuoft Internet Archive].</ref>

<span id='adam_cardelechan'></span>
==== Adam de Cardelechan, burgess of Glasgow, 1285 ====

Adam’s personal locative is ''de Cardelechan''. “Burgess of Glasgow” is civic status, not a Glasgow surname.<ref name="AdamCardelechan">''Registrum Monasterii de Passelet'' (Edinburgh, 1832), p. 399, record of Adam de Cardelechan as burgess of Glasgow.</ref>

<span id='institutional_descriptions'></span>
==== Institutional and diocesan descriptions ====

Forms such as ''episcopus Glasguensis'', ''canonicus Glasguensis'', ''ecclesia Glasguensis'' and “of the church of Glasgow” identify a bishopric, canonry, church, diocese or office. They are not personal surname evidence unless the syntax separately attaches Glasgow to the individual’s name.

This control excludes bishops of Glasgow, canons of Glasgow, Alan the vicar of Glasgow, William de Lamberton as chancellor of the church of Glasgow and other people whose actual personal byname is different.

<small>[[#navigation|↑ Page navigation]] · [[#profiles|Bearer profiles]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='interpretation'></span>
== Interpretation ==

<span id='proved'></span>
=== What is proved ===

# '''Direct personal use before 1300.''' [[#register_pre1300|Twelve working identities]] are securely or highly confidently recorded with Glasgow attached to the person’s name.
# '''Repeated use by the same person.''' [[#william_corbridge|William de Glascou]] appears in 1315 and 1322. [[#master_john|Master John’s]] secure core spans 1377–1384, with probable and later records extending the career. [[#william_physician|William the physician]] appears in 1395 and 1397.
# '''Use independent of venue or office.''' [[#hugh|Hugh]] is called ''de Glasgw'' inside a deed already repeatedly situated in Glasgow. [[#william_corbridge|William]] and [[#master_john|Master John]] retain Glasgow while their clerical offices are separately stated.
# '''Family-identifying use.''' [[#alexander_son_robert|Robert de Glascu]] and [[#john_father_malcolm|John de Glasgu]] are each used to identify a son.
# '''Geographical dispersion.''' The forms occur in Glasgow, Dublin, English royal legal material, Durham, Berwick, Corbridge, Arbroath, Dunkeld, Aberdeen, Moray, Stirling and the Borders.
# '''Late unprefixed forms.''' [[#john_stirling|John Glasgw]] and [[#alan|Alan Glasgw]] show the name without ''de'' in later fifteenth-century records.

<span id='not_proved'></span>
=== What is not proved ===

# [[#alexander_son_robert|Alexander son of Robert]] and [[#john_father_malcolm|Malcolm son of John]] are not independently shown using Glasgow.
# None of the early Robert records is securely joined to another by office, property, associate or relationship.
# [[#john_gamelin|The Gamelin chaplain]] is not demonstrably [[#john_holyrood|the Holyrood John]].
# [[#john_1343|The 1343 John]] is not demonstrably [[#master_john|Master John]].
# [[#matthew|Matthew de Glasgu]] is not demonstrably Matthew de Glendonwyn.
# [[#william_priest|The priest William]] is not demonstrably [[#william_physician|the physician William]].
# [[#john_glasgow_1447|The Glasgow John of 1447–1455]] is not demonstrably [[#john_stirling|the Stirling John of 1475–1479/80]].
# [[#alan|Alan’s 1495 entry]] supplies no pedigree.
# [[#john_alias_smith|The 1506 Smith alias]] does not identify the inherited name.
# Dropping ''de'' does not alone prove surname fixation or hereditary continuity.
# [[#david_provisional|David de Glasgu]] remains a provisional lead because the underlying Lennox act or checkable printed page has not been recovered.
# No single pedigree joins the Dublin, Scottish and northern-English bearers.

<span id='conclusion'></span>
=== Current conclusion ===

The defensible conclusion is narrower and stronger than a general origin story. A Glasgow-derived personal locative was in use by the late twelfth century and was functioning as a stable identifying second name before 1400. Repeated individual use is clear for [[#william_corbridge|William de Glascou]] and [[#master_john|Master John de Glasgow]], and family-identifying use is clear in [[#relationship_records|the Dublin and Scottish father-son formulae]].

Hereditary transmission remains unproved. The evidence may represent one dispersed kindred, several unrelated Glasgow-origin families, or a mixture. The mixed model is presently the least strained: at least two real father-son relationships exist, while the wider corpus shows multiple commercial, civic, royal and ecclesiastical routes through which unrelated people from Glasgow could acquire the same locative.

No search of the present material produced an explicit father–son, sibling or succession formula joining two independently documented pre-1450 bearers. Shared locative, broad region, charter milieu, witness group, seal context or property language can establish association, but none presently establishes descent. [[#david_provisional|David de Glasgu]] adds a useful research lead, not a new branch of a pedigree.

The later fifteenth-century unprefixed forms are consistent with surname stabilisation. They do not bridge the documentary gaps. [[#john_alias_smith|John de Glasgow alias Smith]] in 1506 further warns against treating every occurrence as one continuous surname line.

<small>[[#summary|↑ Research summary]] · [[#navigation|Page navigation]] · [[#top|Top]]</small>

<span id='hypotheses'></span>

<span id='civic_transition'></span>
<span id='sixteenth_century_transition'></span>
== Continuation after 1506 ==

The later fifteenth-century records establish repeated fixed surname forms in Glasgow, Stirling and the Borders, culminating in the 1506 record of [[Space:John Glasgow|John de Glasgow alias Smith]].

The surname therefore remained in documented use into the period covered by Glasgow's surviving burgh protocols. A direct pedigree from the medieval ''de Glasgu'' bearers to the sixteenth-century families has not yet been demonstrated.

Detailed treatment of the later bearers, the first proved Glasgow burgh pedigree, the Corsinkell and Hirmanscheillis households, the family of Robert Glasgow the fisher and the early regional clusters has been moved to:
'''[https://www.wikitree.com/wiki/Space:Glasgow_Branches_in_15th_and_16th_Century_Scotland Early Glasgow Branches in Scotland, c.1447–1650]'''

That page should be used for all post-1506 family reconstruction. This page remains the documentary register for the medieval name and its transition into a settled surname.

== Research hypotheses kept outside the evidential register ==

Norman or Flemish ancestry, Comyn descent, a continuous “House of Walter”, a Duffield-to-Glasgow surname change, an armourer or Smith occupational line, a single war-displacement route and assignment of medieval bearers to modern Y-DNA branches are not established by the records on this page.

These subjects may be explored as separate research hypotheses, but they should not be interwoven with the bearer register unless each step is supported by a document, a proved pedigree or independent converging evidence. Y-DNA can connect documented modern paternal lines and estimate branching periods; it cannot identify [[#roger|Roger]], [[#hugh|Hugh]], [[#master_john|John]], [[#adam_berwick|Adam]] or another named medieval man without a documentary male-line bridge.

Dublin remains the highest-yield institutional cluster. The archive holds the White Book, the Free Citizens roll, city charters and the Guild Merchant Roll.<ref name="DublinHoldings">Dublin City Library and Archive, “About our archive holdings,” describing the Roll of Free Citizens of Dublin, 1225–1250, the White Book, 1230–1603, the Guild Merchant Roll and related civic records; [https://support.librariesireland.ie/hc/en-ie/articles/17350354752145-About-our-archive-holdings Libraries Ireland support site].</ref> The former online medieval databases remain unavailable and the official guidance directs researchers to the Dublin City Library and Archive reading room.<ref name="DublinAssembly">Dublin City Council, “Dublin City Council Databases”, stating that the medieval databases were taken offline on 4 March 2024 and that the material must currently be consulted through the Dublin City Library and Archive reading room; [https://www.dublincity.ie/libraries/heritage-and-history/dublin-city-council-databases Dublin City Council].</ref>

<span id='search_strategy'></span>
=== Search strategy ===

Exact-name searching has diminishing returns because Glasgow frequently appears in institutional phrases. Future work should prioritise:

* associates in the same witness or admission group;
* offices and patrons;
* property succession and neighbouring holdings;
* relationship terms such as ''filius'', ''frater'', ''nepos'', ''gener'', ''heres'', ''uxor'', ''relicta'', ''quondam'', ''executor'' and ''alias'';
* occupational forms such as ''medicus'', ''physicus'', ''clericus'', ''capellanus'', ''mercator'' and ''magister'';
* spelling variants including Glasgu, Glascu, Glasgw, Glasgeu, Glascou, Glasgow, Glasgou, Glasco and OCR forms with long-s confusion.

A parallel rejection register should be maintained for ''Glasguensis'' institutional descriptions, people with another explicit byname, disputed readings and modern surname-summary errors.
